nebula:
C++20 · Qt 6 · macOS · Linux

Nebula Code

An offline-first code editor built with Qt Widgets. Each window combines a folder explorer, tabbed Scintilla editors, and an optional interactive terminal.

Why I built it

I wanted a lightweight desktop editor with familiar development tools and a native C++ foundation.

Editing and workspace tools

  • Split views share documents and undo history, with independent cursor and scroll positions.
  • Quick Open, a command palette, find in files, simultaneous editing, syntax highlighting, and text wrapping.
  • An integrated terminal with configurable docking and persistent workspace sessions.
  • A local Git panel for diffs, staging, unstaging, and commits.
  • On-demand clangd integration for C/C++ completion, navigation, and diagnostics.

Platform support and tradeoffs

Nebula supports Intel and Apple Silicon Macs, plus x86-64 and ARM64 Linux. Git and clangd features use locally installed executables. Large files skip selected language and highlighting features to keep editing responsive.

Measured memory use

The repository reports median process-tree PSS of 35–70 MiB in seven-launch Ubuntu benchmark runs across two file sizes and x86-64 and ARM64. Those measurements use revision 6028b09, before text wrapping was added, and describe that test setup.

meridian:
Linux · Rust · TypeScript

Meridian

A Linux desktop shell with a configurable dock, an app launcher, notifications, and settings for displays, storage, and other hardware.

Problem and contribution

Desktop controls are spread across multiple tools. I built a shell that brings everyday controls into a consistent interface.

Architecture, tradeoffs, and results

I built Meridian to bring desktop controls into one shell. Rust handles system integration, with a TypeScript interface for the dock, launcher, and settings. I used UDisks2 for storage controls and added display hot-plug handling with rollback. Compatibility depends on the available hardware and Wayland compositor protocols.

bluetooth:
macOS · USB HCI · SwiftUI

Raw Bluetooth

An experimental userspace driver that uses an external USB Bluetooth adapter and Google Bumble to connect keyboards and mice to macOS. A SwiftUI app handles scanning, pairing, and saved devices.

Why I built it

I wanted to use Bluetooth keyboards and mice with an external USB adapter through a dedicated macOS app.

How input reaches macOS

  1. The app talks to the external adapter over USB HCI.
  2. Google Bumble discovers and pairs Bluetooth Low Energy devices.
  3. The driver decodes HID reports and forwards keyboard and mouse events to macOS.

Technical decisions and limitations

A userspace approach allows experimentation with the Bluetooth stack and a dedicated interface. It also requires explicit device support and input forwarding; this is not a replacement for every macOS Bluetooth capability.

Test setup

I tested a CSR USB adapter (0a12:0001), a Logitech M196 mouse, and a Logitech K250 keyboard on Intel macOS. Keyboard and mouse input worked on that setup. Audio remains experimental, and compatibility depends on the adapter and peripherals.

wribate:
Next.js · Node.js · MongoDB

Wribate

Problem and contribution

During my internship at Innorize, I helped build a responsive web application for online debate and discussion. I worked on the frontend and REST APIs.

Architecture, tradeoffs, and results

I used Tailwind for the interface, MongoDB for persistence, and JWT authentication for the APIs. Caching and lazy loading improved load speed by about 30% in the project measurements. The résumé figure describes the changes measured during the internship and can vary by page and network.
